sections.h2: Where is Bozeman, Montana, and how is the area set up?
sections.html:
Bozeman is in Gallatin County, in the Gallatin Valley of southwest Montana, at 4,817 feet. It is 84 miles east of Butte, 125 miles west of Billings and 93 miles north of Yellowstone National Park, and Interstate 90 passes through it.

The Bridger Mountains rise to the north-northeast, the Hyalite Peaks of the Gallatin Range to the south, the Spanish Peaks of the Madison Range to the south-southwest and the Tobacco Root Mountains to the west-southwest. The city's land area is about 20.9 square miles, according to Census Bureau figures reported by Wikipedia.

The 2020 census counted 53,293 residents, and the Census Bureau's 2025 estimate is 58,814. The metro area is about 118,960. The city government runs a Community Housing Program, covered below.

sections.h2: What is the history of Bozeman?
sections.html:
John Bozeman opened the Bozeman Trail in 1863, a branch off the Oregon Trail leading to the mining town of Virginia City through the Gallatin Valley. He platted the town with Daniel Rouse and William Beall in August 1864.

  • 1806: William Clark camped east of the future city at the mouth of Kelly Canyon.
  • 1867: Fort Ellis was established nearby.
  • 1883: Bozeman incorporated, with a city council form of government.
  • 1922: Voters adopted the commission and city manager form that the city still uses.

Nelson Story drove about 1,000 head of Longhorn cattle into Paradise Valley in 1866 and later donated land to the state for Montana State University. The valley was called the Valley of the Flowers, and the Crow people held much of it as territory.

Bozeman's top employers include Bozeman Health, Montana State University, Simms Fishing Products and Mystery Ranch. The city also has at least two dozen high-tech firms working on lasers and optical equipment, over a dozen biotech companies and several large software companies.

sections.h2: How does Bozeman's climate affect a house?
sections.html:
Bozeman has a humid continental climate. It receives up to 24 inches of precipitation a year, compared with 8 to 12 inches across much of Montana east of the Continental Divide. That moisture helped give the Gallatin Valley its lush plant growth, which Wikipedia says likely contributed to the choice of Bozeman for Montana State, the state's agricultural college.

  • Winters are cold and snowy, and summers are relatively warm.
  • At this elevation the swing between day and night temperatures can be large.
  • The record high was 105 degrees on July 31, 1892, and the record low was minus 46 degrees, set in 1957 and 1983.

For a seller, snow load on the roof, ice at the eaves and the condition of exterior wood are normal points for a buyer's inspector to check. A house with deferred repairs can be sold as is to a cash buyer rather than repaired before listing.

sections.h2: What schools and roads serve Bozeman?
sections.html:
Almost all of Bozeman is in Bozeman Elementary School District and Bozeman High School District, and a small piece extends into Belgrade's districts. Bozeman Public Schools operates two high schools, Bozeman High and Gallatin High, two middle schools, Chief Joseph and Sacajawea, and eight elementary schools: Emily Dickinson, Hawthorne, Hyalite, Irving, Longfellow, Meadowlark, Morning Star and Whittier.

Interstate 90, U.S. Highway 191 and Montana Highways 86 and 84 are the main roads. Streamline, a zero-fare bus system, was run by the Human Resource Development Council from 2006 until July 1, 2025, when the new Gallatin Valley Urban Transportation District took over. The Skyline bus links Bozeman and Big Sky, and Bozeman Yellowstone International Airport serves travelers to Big Sky, West Yellowstone and Yellowstone National Park.

The Bozeman Fire Department is a full-time career department with 47 uniformed firefighters at three stations, and it responded to about 5,000 emergency calls in 2020.

sections.h2: What is the housing picture in Bozeman?
sections.html:
The City of Bozeman describes housing as a complex challenge that no single program can solve. Its Community Housing Program aims to expand options for people who live, work and study in the city, and it publishes housing data and help resources on its website.

The Regional Housing Coalition's report, Bridging the Gap: A Guide to Funding Affordable Housing in Montana, looks at funding sources for affordable housing in Gallatin County, including tools available locally and ones that would need state action. The program page lists the people it serves: local workers, families, students, seniors, renters, future homeowners and neighborhoods.

We do not quote home values here. If you want a number for your Bozeman house, ask for a written cash offer or request a local appraisal.

sections.h2: Who collects property tax in Bozeman, and when is it due?
sections.html:
The Gallatin County Treasurer collects property tax for Bozeman. The office is at 311 West Main, Room 103, Bozeman, and can be reached at 406-582-3030 or treasurer@gallatin.mt.gov, Monday through Friday from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m. The Department of Revenue's Bozeman office, 406-582-3400, handles questions on market and taxable value.

ItemDetail
2026 real property, first halfDue December 7, 2026, per Gallatin County's iTax site
2026 mobile home, second halfDue November 30, 2026
Standard state scheduleNovember 30 and May 31, each at 5 p.m.
Late payment2% penalty plus 5/6 of 1% interest per month

The county's payment page warns that a mortgage or title company may already be paying on your behalf, so check before paying twice.

The 2026 state rates are tiered for primary residences and long-term rentals, starting at 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value. Second homes, short-term rentals and vacant residential lots pay a flat 1.90%, and the Department notes that VRBO and Airbnb type rentals are in the higher class. Anyone who owns a Bozeman-area second home or short-term rental should look at that rate before deciding to hold or sell.

sections.h2: How do you sell a house fast in Bozeman?
sections.html:
The three options are an agent listing, a sale by owner or a cash offer. A listing exposes the house to more buyers but adds showings, commission and negotiation after inspection. A sale by owner saves commission and leaves the paperwork to you. A cash offer is typically as is and closes on a date you choose.

Montana's transfer steps are the same either way. The deed must be acknowledged before a notary, filed with the Gallatin County Clerk and Recorder with a Realty Transfer Certificate, and recorded for the standard fee of $20 for the first page and $10 for each added page. Unpaid property tax is a lien and is settled at closing.

If you want to sell your Bozeman house for cash, send the address through the form above. We reply with a written offer, and you owe nothing if you decline.

faqs.q: How far is Bozeman from other Montana cities?
faqs.a: Bozeman is 84 miles east of Butte and 125 miles west of Billings, and it is 93 miles north of Yellowstone National Park.

faqs.q: Who collects property tax in Bozeman?
faqs.a: The Gallatin County Treasurer, at 311 West Main, Room 103. The Department of Revenue's Bozeman office handles questions about market and taxable value.

faqs.q: What is the 2026 property tax rate on a Bozeman primary residence?
faqs.a: A tiered rate: 0.76% on the first $378,000 of market value, 0.90% from $378,001 to $756,000, 1.10% from $756,001 to $1,511,999 and 1.90% above that. Second homes and short-term rentals pay a flat 1.90%.
Almost all of Bozeman is in Bozeman Elementary and Bozeman High School Districts. A small area is in the Belgrade districts.

faqs.q: Can I sell my Bozeman house as is?
faqs.a: Yes. A cash buyer can purchase a Bozeman house in its present condition. The sale still needs a notarized deed, a Realty Transfer Certificate and recording with the county clerk and recorder.
